life_summary: Richard Louis Evans was born in 1906 in Salt Lake City, Utah. He grew up in the early twentieth-century LDS community and developed a distinctive gift for public communication and broadcasting. Evans received his education in Salt Lake Valley schools and pursued studies in music and communications. He became a prominent voice in religious broadcasting during the golden age of radio, developing a distinctive style of spiritual commentary that appealed to both Church members and the broader American public. Evans married and established a family while building his career in communications. His talent for translating religious concepts into language accessible to mainstream audiences made him a unique figure in twentieth-century LDS leadership.
church_summary: Evans served as a missionary in European missions during his youth. He became best known for his role as the host and narrator of the Tabernacle Choir at Temple Square radio program, one of the longest-running radio programs in American broadcasting history. He was ordained as a member of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles and served in that capacity for many years, bringing his communication expertise to apostolic ministry. Evans was deeply involved in transmitting LDS messages through the modern media of radio and television, helping the Church reach millions of Americans during the twentieth century. His distinctive voice and thoughtful presentation of doctrine made him one of the most recognizable LDS leaders of his era.
